chief_complaint: crushing chest pain, sweating, and difficulty breathing 3 hours after husband's sudden death
hpi_details: Presents via emergency ambulance with acute, severe, crushing substernal chest pain 9/10 radiating to her neck and left shoulder, accompanied by acute shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and nausea. Symptoms began abruptly 3 hours after she witnessed her husband of 40 years collapse and die suddenly from a cardiac arrest at home. She has no prior personal history of heart disease, hypertension, or diabetes.

social_hx: non-smoker, zero alcohol, retired music teacher, newly bereaved

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes that initial management mirrors acute coronary syndrome until emergency coronary angiography rules out obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: crushing chest pain, sweating, and difficulty breathing 3 hours after husband's sudden death

Key HPI features: Presents via emergency ambulance with acute, severe, crushing substernal chest pain 9/10 radiating to her neck and left shoulder, accompanied by acute shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and nausea. Symptoms began abruptly 3 hours after she witnessed her husband of 40 years collapse and die suddenly from a cardiac arrest at home. She has no prior personal history of heart disease, hypertension, or diabetes.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 112, BP 105/65, O2 sat 93% on air. 12-lead ECG: prominent ST-segment elevation across anterior and precordial leads (V1-V6) mimicking anterior STEMI, plus QT prolongation. Bloods: high-sensitivity troponin mildly/moderately elevated (typically lower than expected for the extensive degree of ECG/echocardiographic wall motion abnormality), BNP elevated. Emergency coronary angiography: reveals completely normal, patent epicardial coronary arteries without plaque or thrombus. Left ventriculogram and Echocardiogram: demonstrates characteristic apical ballooning with severe akinesia/dyskinesia of the mid and apical left ventricle and hyperkinesia of the basal segments (resembling a Japanese octopus trap - takotsubo).
Relevant background/PMH: mild generalized anxiety, zero cardiovascular risk factors or prior angina
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to ST-elevation myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: It is indistinguishable from a myocardial infarction on presentation — treat as ACS.
management_principles: Initial management mirrors acute coronary syndrome until emergency coronary angiography rules out obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease
Once confirmed: inpatient cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias (long QT / torsades de pointes risk) and cardiogenic shock
Initiate supportive heart failure medical therapy (ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker) to aid left ventricular recovery and blunt catecholamine surge
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 63F postmenopausal female presents with acute severe crushing chest pain, dyspnoea, and diaphoresis immediately following severe acute emotional distress (bereavement).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 112, BP 105/65, O2 sat 93% on air. 12-lead ECG: prominent ST-segment elevation across anterior and precordial leads (V1-V6) mimicking anterior STEMI, plus QT prolongation. Bloods: high-sensitivity troponin mildly/moderately elevated (typically lower than expected for the extensive degree of ECG/echocardiographic wall motion abnormality), BNP elevated. Emergency coronary angiography: reveals completely normal, patent epicardial coronary arteries without plaque or thrombus. Left ventriculogram and Echocardiogram: demonstrates characteristic apical ballooning with severe akinesia/dyskinesia of the mid and apical left ventricle and hyperkinesia of the basal segments (resembling a Japanese octopus trap - takotsubo).
reference_soap.assessment: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy (Broken Heart Syndrome / Stress-Induced Cardiomyopathy). DDx: acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to plaque rupture, coronary artery spasm (Prinzmetal), acute myocarditis, phaeochromocytoma crisis.
reference_soap.plan: Initial management mirrors acute coronary syndrome until emergency coronary angiography rules out obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease. Once confirmed: inpatient cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias (long QT / torsades de pointes risk) and cardiogenic shock. Initiate supportive heart failure medical therapy (ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker) to aid left ventricular recovery and blunt catecholamine surge. Provide specialized psychological and bereavement counseling. Reassure patient that left ventricular function typically recovers completely within 4 to 8 weeks with supportive care.

learning_objectives: Recognise the classic epidemiological and emotional triggers of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: postmenopausal female experiencing profound acute emotional/physical stress
Identify the clinical paradox: STEMI-like ECG and extensive apical ballooning akinesia in the presence of completely normal angiographic coronary arteries
Explain the pathophysiological mechanism of catecholamine surge toxicity affecting beta-adrenoceptor density at the left ventricular apex
Formulate compassionate, empathetic communication bridging emergency acute cardiac stabilization with bereavement support

teaching.one_liner: Severe emotional stress stuns the left ventricle, mimicking a heart attack exactly — the history of a preceding shock is the clue.
red_flags: It is indistinguishable from a myocardial infarction on presentation — treat as ACS

must_ask.say: Did anything very stressful happen just before this started?

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?
Along with the pain, did you feel sweaty, sick, or short of breath?

must_ask.objective: Cardiac risk factors — often absent here
must_ask.say: Do you have any heart problems, high blood pressure or diabetes?
How are you coping, and who do you have around you?

history.answer: I have this crushing, unbearable chest pain, and I can hardly catch my breath.
It hit me completely out of the blue about three hours ago, right after my husband suddenly collapsed and passed away in front of me.
It feels like it is deep in the middle of my chest, right behind my breastbone. It is across my whole chest, so I cannot point to it with just one finger.
It is a severe, heavy, crushing sensation, like a vice clamping down or an elephant sitting on my chest.
Yes, the crushing ache shoots straight up into my neck and spreads down into my left shoulder.
It has been non-stop and relentless since it started three hours ago. It has not eased up for even a second.
It is easily a 9 out of 10. It is the most intense, terrifying pain I have ever experienced.
I was just sitting on the floor waiting for the paramedics when it started, and resting has not helped at all.
No, taking a deep breath, coughing, or moving around does not change the pain, and pressing on my chest does not make it hurt worse.
No, I have not eaten anything since breakfast hours before this happened, and there is no heartburn, acid, or trouble swallowing.
Yes, I started sweating profusely, breaking out in cold sweats, and feeling terribly short of breath the moment the chest pain hit.
I feel very sick to my stomach and nauseated, but I have not thrown up, and I have not passed out.
No fever, no chills, and no cough or mucus at all.
No, I have been completely well and have not had any cold, flu, or viral infection lately.
No, neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I have not had any surgery or long plane travel recently.
No, there are no rashes, bumps, or blisters on my chest or anywhere else.
I feel an overwhelming sense of doom and sheer terror, like my life is slipping away right now. My hands feel clammy, but they are not tingling.
My husband of forty years had a sudden cardiac arrest right in our living room three hours ago. The shock and grief hit me like a physical wave.
Never. I have never had angina, chest pressure, or heart trouble before in my life.
No, I have never had a heart attack, an angiogram, or a stent.
No, I have not had any fall, injury, or heavy physical strain to my chest.
No doctor has ever told me I had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart problems.
I honestly feel like the shock and heartbreak literally broke my heart into pieces.
I am terrified that I am having a fatal heart attack on the very same day my husband died.
Please do whatever emergency treatment is needed to keep me alive. I cannot leave my grieving children alone today.
I only have mild generalized anxiety from time to time. Otherwise, I have always been healthy.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy when I was a teenager, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, and I have not taken any over-the-counter painkillers or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I do not drink alcohol.
I am a retired elementary school music teacher. I live in our family home, and our two adult children are rushing here now.
There is no history of early heart attacks or sudden cardiac deaths in my parents or siblings.
I went through menopause naturally over ten years ago and have never taken hormone replacement therapy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, temperature 36.8°C.
Anxious-appearing female in acute distress, pale, visibly diaphoretic, and clutching her chest.
Normal chest wall contour with no reproducible tenderness, swelling, or localized wall pain upon palpation.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle without distension.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Mild bilateral fine inspiratory crackles at the lung bases; no wheezes or pleural friction rubs.
Cool, pale, and diaphoretic skin with no rashes, vesicles, or localized chest lesions.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without epigastric pain or organomegaly.
No pitting edema in the lower extremities bilaterally.
Calves are symmetric and supple with no warmth, swelling, or calf tenderness bilaterally.
